From the Kilmarnock Juurnal, April 15. CHINA. ATTACK ON CHUENPKK AND TYKOK'TO W FORTS. From some loose notes with which we have been kindly favoured we have it now in our power to lay before our local readers rough a account of the plan of attack on the Chuenpec and Tvkoktow foils ; and, if they will have the kindness to recall to their remembrance the relations of place and distance of Chucnpee and its neighbourhood, we hope to be able t<> couvey to them by our descriptions a toler-

331iT5T©3 /""HS ably correct idea of the scenes at Chuen pee on the 7th inst The boats were manned and armed, and the Royal Maiineso! the squad von, under Captain Lilts, were ready to land on ihe morning of the 7lh. The detachments of the 26th and 49th Regiments, 37th Madras Native Infantry and Bengal Volunteers, em harked on hoard the steamers Enterprise and Madagascar, and were conveyed to the point of debarkation and landed in the transport's boats Captain Knowles commanded the artillery, having under him Lieutenant the Hon. Spenser ; the force of this arm consisted of two 24 pounder howitzers and two 6 pound' er guns ; the guns were worked by the artillery men, but to each howitzer 30 seamen of the Blenheim were attached, and to the 6 pounder 15 seamen of the ships from w hich they were landed, to drag them into position The guns were placed on the ridge of a lull commanding the entrenchment. The Queen and Nemesis took op a position within good shell distance, as the depth of water allowed, an I attacked the fort on the hil', which was soon deserted. The Callope, Hyacinth, and Lame, weight d and proceeded above the Latteries to be ready to attack in that quarter, and to capture the junks. Captain Herbert commanded this portion of the force The Samarang, Druid. Columbine and Modest e, were ordered to make a simultaneous attack on i'vkoktow, the object being to dismantle the fort. Capt Scott had charge of this dm ston. The Madagascar and Enterprise ha v ing landed their troops proceeded to join the

Calliope's division. All the dispositions having been made, and the troops landed a little to the southward of the island, they "formed, and pushed strong covering parties in advance of the guns, and then waited the effect of their fire, as weli as that ot the squadron ; thev then marched in two bodies on ihe hill fort, into which the Queen and Nemesis had previously thrown some shells; on reaching the intervening valley the stockade opened a fire on the troops ; but was soon silenced by the field pieces, placed, as noticed above, on the edge ol the hill ; the troops (the Cameronians and Marines) then pushed forwaid up the hill, and took possession of the fort, whilst the Bengal Volunteers and 57th Madras Native infantry debouched from the valley to the northward, ami then, left shoulders forward, marched round the hill. After driving the Chinese, who made a handsome defence, out of the stockade, the Cameronians and Marines deployed, and rushed down the hill on the iower'and largest fort, enteied the embrasures, and drove all before them, the garrison escaping through the northern gate, when they were iuten upted in their sauve qui peut re treat by the native troops which had debouched from the valley, who opened a most de structive fire upon them ; this spot, a short distance from the northern gate and beach, was the slaughterhouse ; it was here the hiptae, a mandarin of the third class, was killed, obstinately lefusing quarter from a sergeant nt marines, who ran up to him as his people

were carrying him off severely wounded þÿ He cut at the sergeant, who parried the blow with his bayonet, and nearly had the worst of the encounter. 'I he Chinese, with the Came" ronians and Marines in their rear, and the native troops in front, rushed into t he Water to escape, but there fell beneath the united fire of the troops It should be here remarked, that the Chinese do not understand either giving or taking quarter in the European military sense of those conditions ; many of the

Chinese, when in the water, fiied their matchlocks at the naiive troops, and then threw them awav and made no submission ; hut this hit and fall down proceeding the Sepoys did not understand, but returned the fire of the Chinese þÿ of course with fatal effect. The left di> ision led in splendid style by the Druid, Captain Smiih, were in their stations about half past 10 o'clock a. m. The Druid reserving tier fire, although a brisk cannonade was k'-pt up from ibis extensive fori until she dropt tier anchor, when instantly she poured in a destructive þÿbroadside her example being followed by the other ships, as they came up in succession. A landing was effected to siorm i fie foil, but the Chinese obstinately defended themselves at the north gate, being driven by the broadsides fiom the batteries, hut not until a great many of 'their guns were dismounted or rendered unserviceable. Several peisonal encounters here took place, and to show the obstinacy of their defence, a mandarin having lost his arms, grappled with an officer of t lie Modesle. and bit liirn severely in the arm. The Columbine being on the flank, her batteries enfilading the fort, threw in upon the enemy , who were now fil ing and reining, a destructive discharge of grape and canuister. In an hour the British flag floated over the fort. The enemy's loss was great, hut we are unable to speak accurately as to number. Here, as at Chuenpce. the clothea (padded with cotton) of the killed and wounded as thev fell, were ignited by their matches

and ammunition boxes, which they carry in front, and ihe bodies almost consumed by fiie# Thus tell ihe forts, stockades, and garrisons of Chuenpec and Tykoktow to her Biitannic Majesty's arms on the 7th Januaty 1841 þÿ The stockades were well and strongly built, but their situation was not well selected, being commanded l.y the neighbouring lulls. '1 hey afford a proof ol the advance the Chinese have made m the means of defence. From the freshness of the materials employed in their construction it would appear that they have heen erected within these few weeks, while the British I'lenipotentiaiy has heen negotiating; and, had thev heen held by detei mined men, or rather skilful soldieis, it would have cost our troops some trouble to have taken them. As it w as the niaru.es had a good manv men wounded in the attack ; and, although exposed to a heavy and galling fite fiom the field pieces and musketry, the Chinese resolutely defended them for twenty minutes, and it was only a forward movement of the gallant and evei distinguished Canieronians þÿ not invalids, as have been elsewhere most egregiously misnamed þÿ and marines that induced them to evacuate the works The deep dry ditch and breast-work of these defences ofler. ing no small obstacles to our attacking force. Some amusing scenes ocouried whilst our men wete struggling who should be the firs up the steep and hard clay sidi s ol the dry ditch, proving how totally reckless are British soldiers and sailors " in the day and hour

of danger '' During the attack Major J'ratt, of the Camernniatis, was seen a long way in advance, under the very defence of the enemy, with admirable coolness quietly reconnoitring their position. 'I lie gallant Major, on looking through one of the embrasures saw there was a body of Chinese close to it, when fie coolly turned to the only soldier with him a marine, and said, " Just shoot me one of these fellows, will you?" The action followed the word, and the rest of the Cninesc forthwith retired to a more respectful distance.

W< do not expect to find in ilie construction nl Chinese forts anv exhibition ol engineering skill ; they have not had a Vauhan. It ap pears, however, that the materials they employ for the upper part of their works, such as paraphets, embrasures, 61 c., are par'iculaily well chosen for the purpose, t appears to he a composition like chunam, upon whteh our shot made hut very little impression. Most of the Chinese guns were of small calibre, the metal wretched iron, and as wretchedly manufactu" red, a single blow of a hammer being sudi cient to knock off the trunnions ; they were spiked or otherwise destroyed, and most of them were thrown into the sea : the carriages were all burnt, the breastwork and ditches of the stockades escaped with only partial dismantling, but every thing within them has been totally destroyed hy fire, and the guns removed, with the exception of a long Spanish piece of larger calibre than usual, which is lying dismounted at a Hanking breast- work commanding the approach from the valley at the base ol the lull. Had this formidable gun been well served, its shot would have mowed down many of the gallant Cameronians and marines The sites of houses and huts are now only to tie distinguished by smoking ru ns. The ground over the whole extent of the fortifications is thickly strewn with tattered remnants of clothes. <fcc. ; the Chinese snliered horribly from falling, when wounded, I 011 their burning matches, which set fire to their padded cotton garments and powder

fl-isks, which they wear round the waist, and literally blew them tip, and burnt them slowly to death The burial ot these black, mangled corpses, was a fearful spectacle. The beach running fiom Chuenpee fort down into Anson's Bay is strewn with the eharred timbers of the junks so effectually destroyed b\ the JS tmesis and the boais of the squadron, among which many Chinese corpses are vet lying, Jan lg, 13, and 14 Many of the bodies were large and athietic, much beyond the generality of the natives of this province. þÿ J est over the brow of the rising ground at the the landing place id the Chuenpee fort, great numbers of the dead lie buried in one large common grave, over whom some carelessthoughtless "jolly jac k lat" has raised a hoard " This is the road to glory." bearing the following inspiriting inscription : ' he poorer natives do u" show any fear at our having taken Chuenpee; numbers of boats are about the fleet, and m many instances the Chinese have returned to seek the bodies of their slain relations. which they have exhumed, and although in a state of decomposition, they are carrying the bodies away in great numbers. But among these exhibitions ot filial and fraternal feeling there have been some impostors, seeking their young brothers." evidently trying " to excite the compassion of the officers Provisions ate easily procurable. Une oid man and woman the only natives left on the island ; they were on the point where death was rifest. but would not abandon the hearth ot their

fathers The old man was slightly wounded, but is under the care, as are many of t tie wounded Chinese, of our suigeons. Great praise is due to those geiroiiien for the humane attention they bes»' bed, as far as was in their power, on the w tinted sons of Ham The following anecdote exhibits the base cunning and callouq leartlessness of the Chi. tiesc character A" chaige was brought bv tliein against some of our men for murdering a man; the chaige, however, upon investigation, was proved to be uuluuuded, and that,

EarZEMmTDS instead of a man, it was a bullock that had been murdered The Chinese said they could procure the body of the murdered man in prool of their charge ; they were required to do so. when they brought a corpse in a state of decomposition, which had evidently been procured tor occasion from the graves in the fort. We have heard of similar charges having been made, and similar proofs having been exhibited, more than once at Whatnpoa many years ago When a place is carried by storm it is always given up to plunder but there was nothing found in the Chuenpee lort hot a few cloaks and raps, yet one thing was discovered which, although it may surprise some, will not surprise others þÿ about 100 balls of the "foreign smoke" were found, ft is probable the spirits of the Chinese were exalted to the gallant resistance they opposed to our troops fry a tew additional pipes or pills of this stimulant ; and it such was the effect, we think neither the Emperor nor his commissioner will blame its use- on that occasion.

from the New York Albion, May 22, 1841. PROCEEDINGS IN THE CASE OF .VI K. Mc'LEOD. The case of Mr. Mc'Leod was called on in the Supreme Court of this city on Monday last, the 17th inst , and simple as it seems to us, it is likely to be prolonged an indefinite but tiresome extent. At the commencement of the proceedings, Mr. Mc'Leod by his counsel put in an affidavit to the following effect ; viz , That in December 1837, a body of about 300 men proceeded from the State of .New York and took forcible possession of Navy Island, and there assumed a hostile position, against the dominions of the Queen ; that these occupants of Navy Island were to a great extent citizens of the United Stales, and were commanded by one liensellaer, also a citizen of the United States, and that they were supplied with provisions and arms from the United States, and from the citizens thereof. That, to repel this iuvasion an army of about 2a00 men was assembled at Chippewa by order of the Provincial Government, and that a frequent cannonade was kept up between that army and the invaders, and that the support which the latter received from the citizens and residents of the United States prevented the army from the prompt execution of their purpose. That the Caroline steamboat was constantly employed in proceeding to and from Schlosser, in the United States, and Navy Island, transporting provisions and implements of war in aid of the invaders at the said island, and that on the 29th December, 1837, she made several tiips between the two places. That on the

following evening several boats and men armed, were fitted out at Chippewa by order of Colonel Mc'Nab, who was lawfully in com mand of Her Majesty's forces there, with orders to take and destroy the said steamboat ; that this command was executed, the expedition having expelled those who occupied the boat, then destroyed her That Amos Durfee, as he is informed and bdieves, was killed in the attack and not at any other time The affidavit further sets forth, that he is indicted as an accessory before the fact in what the indictment calls the murder of Durfee, but not for having any agency in the death ot that person in any other manner than as one of the party in the expedition ; and after alluding to the correspondence of the two governments on the subject, and the matter becoming a public and national consideration, Mr. Mc Ltod concludes by a solemn denial that he was present at all at the expedition against the Caroline or the killing of Durfee. Mr. McLeod's counsel next read copious extracts from the correspondence between the British Minister Mr. Fox, and several officers of state of the United States in relation to the subject, and also from other official correspondence which related thereto, most of which has already at various times been published in the journals ; but the following note from Mr. Fox to Mr. Webster, dated 12th March, 1841, being of so much importance in the case may here have place. " Her Majesty's Government have had under consideration the subject of the arrest and

imprisonment of Alexander McLeod, on a pretended charge ol arson and murder, and I am directed to make known to the Govern, ment of the U S. that the British Government entirely approved of the course pursued, by him. 1 am instructed to demand formally and in the name of the British Government,

a&wsx; T-ssmrassa S'-s c satBttrrpa the immediate release of Alexandor McLeod, 'or the reason that the transaction was one of a public character, planned and executed by persons duly authorized bv the Colonial Government, to take such measures as may bo necessary for protecting the property and lives of her Majesty's subjects, and being therefore an act of public duty, they cannot be held responsible to the laws and tribunals of any foreign country." The counsel for the prosecution then put in a Demurrer to the effect that the Caroline was a peaceful vessel at anchor in a place belonging to the United States ; that Col. Mc'Nab had no right to send an expedition there; that Amos Durfee was unconnected with the in surgents at Navy Island, nor guilty ot offence against Great Britain, and was killed on the mainland of the United States ; and that Mr. McLeod has pleaded, to the indictment preferred agamst him, his plea being " Not Guilty." On Tuesday the 18th, the case was continued ; the District Attorney for Niagara ! countv, read several depositions to the following effect: viz þÿ 1. One by Captain Gilbert Appleby who deposed that Mr. VlcLeod was on hoard the Caroline on the night ot the ex pedition, and made a thirst at the deponent with a sword. That he was less confident now than he was at the. time that the prisoner was Mr. McLeod. 2. One by Leonard Anson, who deposed that he had heard Mr McLeod boast of having killed one American in that expedition. 3 One by Norman Barnam, who deposed that he had heard Mr.

McLeod boast that his sword had drank the biood of two. at that expedition. Other documents and evidences were read, and the Attorney General then contended that sufficient evidence had been tendered to make a prima facie case On the part of Mr McLeod it was argued that this was the first attempt ever made to hold individuals personally responsible for acts done in obedience to the orders of legal autho rities. and the grouud was learnedly and forcibly gone over of the international law in such cases The counsel then adverted io that part of the Demurrer which relates to the fact ol Durfee being killed on shore by a shot and not on board in the fray ; and he argued that the death of Durfee was a part of the general cousequeuce of the attack on the Caroline. One of the counsel for the prosecution agreed that it was no matter how the Caroline was occupied or engaged, nor how publicly the laet was known ; that she was anchored or moored in American waters ought to have been sufficient security against such an attack as that expedition. Tht Counsel was followed by the Attorney General who avowed his opinion of the competency to proceed in the trial by indictment, inasmuch as Mr. Mc Leod had pleaded thereto. On the other hand it is contended that the State of New York cannot take cognizance of an offence against the entire American nation ; that the power to make war or peace lies with Congress or the general government ; that the act in which the prisoner is alleged to

have participated is one publicly authorized ; that if it were an offence cognizable hv the U S Courts, the trial of an individual would be incompatible with the pending negociations between the two governments, and are at once unworthy of the honor und dignity of both.

It is thought that the court will not decide this important case before the end of the present term. The fo'lowing are the points of greatest moment which on the Habeas Corpus tend most favorable in Mr. McLeod's case. 1 When acts are done under the commands of duly constituted public authority the party acting in obedience thereto cannot be personally responsible for such obedience. 2. The Supreme Court has jurisdiction to try the alleged offence, and may try it at Bar. It is, therefore, competent to advise the District Attorney to order a nolle prosequi upon j the indictment. 3. Kedress having been demanded on this ground, and being now the subject of negotiation between the two governments, the State of New York can neither directly nor lawtully interpose its jurisdiction in the case. In short, as was forcibly observed by Mr. Spencer, one ol Mr McLeod's Counsel, the Court in acting upon the case would incur a fearful responsibility, and on their decision alone might learn the great question of peace or war with Great Biitaui. The learned gentleman adverted to the anxiety with which its action was observed by the national Government, as to wtiicii he bad no authority to declare tnal it desired the release of Mr. Mc Lend; but be might say that every facility hail been given to his counsel, every application of theirs for information had been promptly and luily complied with, and lie lelt assured that the government of the United States awaited the result, with anxiety yet with con-

fidence that this State would do right ; and in doing so would free the prisoner. He alluded to the many points of dispute arid difficulty existing between the two countries, and deprecaied the addition ot this, which would be the worst and most difficult of ail. as most nearly touching the leelings ol the British people. W hilsi the above proceedings were in progress in tins city, a message from the Governor of the Mate was received by the Assembly in \lbany, communicating a copy of official correspondence between the department of the State and the United States on the subject of Mr. McLeod; stating likewise that no arrangements had been entered into with the United States respecting that individual ; that he is now before the Supreme Court of the State on a writ of Habeas Votpus, sued out by himself with a view to his discharge; that the department had no knowledge or privity concerning the application ; that upon learning the matter incidentally, instructions were given to the Attorney General to resist the motion for the prisoner's discharge ; and concluded by assuring the Assembly that nothing should be done, with the consent of the department, tending tocomprimit the rights, dignity, and honour of the State. The proceedings in the case so far, have resulted in an order of the Court, that Mr Mc Leod be committed to the custody of the Sheriff of New York, and that the Sheriff of Niagara Co. be no longer chargeable with the said custody.

St. Croix Chrisliansted, Thursday June 24, 1841- The London Times of the 19th ultimo contains the cl >se of the Debate on the Sugar duties hill, which lasted ten nights, and elicited elaborate speeches from all the leading orators of both parties. The whole ground of free trade, prohibition and protection, was explored, and no question yet discussed in Parliament appears to have created more interest, or excitement. Sir 14. Peel did not speak until the last night, and he, having adroitly selected the weak part of his opponents arguments, for attack. (the encouragement of foreign slavery, and the discouragement to their own colonies, which would result from the success of tiie ministerial proposition,) his speech had a powerful effect on the final vote, which stood as follows, For the ministerial proposition to reduce the foreign duty on Sugar from '03s to 36s 281 against it 317 a

598 leaving a majority of 36 against the ministers, several ot whom admitted, that their opponents would probably be soon in their places. This question being decided in a very lull house will not. it is supposed, be again brought up. unless ministers should he willing to lower their own Colonial duty to 12 or 15s, which, however, they think would create too great a loss to the revenue, but which others are of opinion, would he made up bv the increased consumption of sugar. Ministers stand no chance of success in their other proposition to alter the Lorn laws, in which they vill be left in a still smaller minority Sir A. Grant stated tfiat Sugar made by tree labor costs 12s per 1 001 b more than that made from slave labor The second May packet was detained four days to bring out the result of the above debate on the Sugar duties The American Ship Win. Brown sailed from Liverpool for New York late in March last, run upon Icebergs, and sunk, leaving just time for the passengers and crew, about 40 in number, to get into the boats, which however were not sufficient to hold them, and melancholy to stale, 14 of the most exhausted of the number, were thrown ovei board! among tliein, a young man who had a sister in the boat, and who, on seeing her brother thrown overboai d, immediately plunged in to the waves after him, tiiere finding a watery grave ; the next day they fell in with an American Ship, who took them on board and carried them to Havre. Another British ship from South America with -!a valuable cargo

and 4120,00 in specie, was run on board by an American ship, near the English coast, and sunk, eight of her crew lost their lives, the residue being picked up, Captain Hosken of the Great Western writes that lie never knew of so much ice in the Atlantic, having found it difficult in his last passage to steer clear of it. From the Kilmarnock Journal, April 15. NIGER EXPEDITION. We have often had occasion to notice the munificence and liberality of the illustrious Consort of our Queen, but rarely have we hoard of an incident rpnre illustrative of the good taSie and sympathetic feeling of his Koval Highness than that which we have now the pleasure of communicating. It is well known that his Koval Highness not long since visited and minutely inspected her þÿMajesty steam-vessels, s when being fitted out for the Niger expedition. On that occasion, the Prince exhibited the greatest interest in the scientific arrangements of L)r. Reid for preserving the health of their crews, and entered with great urbanity into the provisions that were made for the comfort of all who are to accompany the expedition. The interest of his Koval Highness in this great national undertaking has not, however, terminated here, his Koval Highness having within the«e few days presented to the commanders of the Albert, the Wilber force, and the London respectively, a highly finished gold pocket chronometer, as a mark of the unabated anxiety he feels for the success of the enterpi ise. The following inscription exhibits the occasion on which these valuable gifts have been presented, honourable alike to the Prince, and to the officers on whom this great undertaking devolves ; and we will only add. that with the most becoming good taste, the instruments has been prepared by three of the first-rate makers in London : þÿ þÿ Presented by his Koval Highness Prince
Albert , of her þÿMajesty s steamer on his departure with the expedition to the Niger, for the abolition of the slave trade.-- March 23, þÿ1841. þÿ .Morning Chronicle,

ROMANCE IN REAL LIFE. The following details are as strange as they are true. In the neighbourhood of Gloucester, a young lady, of highly respectable connexions, has experienced a series of reverses in the cause of the þÿheart slast affection seldom equalled A gentleman, of some station in society, became by accident acquainted with the maiden to whom we allude, and their affection becoming reciprocal, the day was fixed for their union, which was to have taken place in the city of Gloucester. Agreeably with this arrangement, and as the match was a desirable one, her parent parted with a lucrative business in the country, on Which she and her mother lived in respectability and comfort, and went to Gloucester, intending to settle. The day for the celebration of the wedding arrived ; but, alas ! the bridegroom came not : his parents had peicmptnrily forbidden the match, and he was already, by their contrivance, on the seas, bound for Jamaica. A letter reached the poor girl, but to confirm her tears ; his þÿparents consent had been withheld, and he had suddenly left the seaport town in the West of Englandt where he resided, not a faithless, but an nn happy lover. Time passed, and industry on the part of the hapless girl but ill supplied the loss of the comparative independence herself and family had left when they came to the city of Gloucester, with the views, and indulging the hopes to which we have alluded, and though blighted in heart, she cheerfully succeeded in helping to support her decrepit

»>AW33R TJBOTSIS T1E)13X mother and aunt in comfort. Time, the gentle softener of affliction had many a long day cast its dimming shadow over the great event of her life, and nothing more had been heard of her absent lover, till a week or two ago, when, to her astonishment and delight, she received a letter from him, breathing the devotedness of constant attachment, and vows ot unaltered affection, not the less welcome, though wafted across the sens. Another and another followed begging forgiveness for the former apparent neglect þÿ and still another, the last accompanied by the consent of the parents of the .absent one. DISPUTE WITH AMERICA. The following ternarks on this subject are taken from the Hxaminer. þÿ What increases our regret at the present difference between the countries is the worthlessness of the questions in dispute. We are debating, whether the boundaries of terrilories already too vast lor the inhabitants, shall run for 100 miles in one direction or in another; and whether an act done in 1S37 was or was not slriplly legal. All sensible persons on both sides of the water must say þÿ Let the questions be referred, or deferred, or settled ni any way whatever compatible with our honour, so that we way hear no more of them, and return to the confident intercourse on which the prosperity of both countries depends. Austria, or France, or any other military non commercial State, mav waste its sources in war or angry diplomacy, hut such luxuries do not suit nations of '^agriculturalists, manufacturers, and merchants. Six months of alarm and suspense cost us as much as a little war."

From the New York Weekly Herald, May 25. THE MCLEOD CASE. The question coming on to day, and to be discussed and decided in the Supreme Court of the Stale of New York, holding its present term in this city, m the case of Alexander McLeod excites i he most intense and general interest. This is not surprising, for probably no question ever came before a high State tribunal in this country more profoundly important. Its intrinsic difficulties are i numerous and perplexing, but the high na- ! tional interests, honor, pride and feeling which are involved in its determination add to the delicacy and dillicuity of the discussion. Liberty is of no value if it is to be qualified bv ihe dictation of foreign powcis If the course of law is to be diverted or impaired, by a pliant legislature or a servile judiciary, the protection of law is at an end, and we might as well dissolve the hands which unite us together in society, and return to a state of nature. But we are proud to believe, troin the course winch the Legislature, die Judiciary and the people have taken in this matter) that no such baleful events await us. In the faithful and luminous minds, to which the case is now to he presented, we are happy to recognize the long tried and trusty qualities which have hitherto maintained the integ. rity of die laws and on which we still confi denily rely for their honest and undaunted exposition. The proceeding on which this question is now brought up. is strictly conformable to law, and is in fact the very course which ought to he pursued, tor the purpose of uis posing of the main difficulty in the case. The present object is not the trial of McLeod for the offence with which he is charged, hut simply to determine by a judicial examination, whether die (act of his having acied under the orders of sujierior officers, who de rived their authority from the British Govern ment, in Ins participation in the attack upon j the Caroline, consti utes under all the cir-

cumstances of the case, a good reason whv he should be set free and not tried lor murder at all, 1 his is the main, and probably the only distinct question to be atgued, but from its nature and importance it must necessarily lead to many cullateial discussions. But that this latter can be completely imparted to cold water by simply soaking the pieces of dried canes in it, seems rather doubtful. The canes must either be left lo soak a very considerable period of time, or some means must he used thoroughly to macerate them before the liquid is strained. It mav be thought presumptuous in us perhaps to doubt that which has been done, but as matteis now stand, we do doubt the practicability of procuring more sugar from a given quantity ot canes in the manner stated, than could be by the old process Bv the wav, might not an addition to ihe sugar crop be made bv throwing the trash immediately as it is taken from the mill into clean water, evaporating it by boiling in the wav stated. Warming on her passage from Copenhagen to St. Croix, North of Scotland and Ireland, in latitude 53" 34' and longitude 12 30' west, on the 10th of April 1811, discovered a wreck with her masts and bowsprit gone, her hull only three feet above water Captain Warming immediately bore down upon her, in order to see if there was anv human being on hoard to be saved, and to examine her condition. þÿ She was found full of water, of about 300 tons burthen, and the only name yet to be discovered on her stern was þÿ þÿLondon, the rest being washed out bv the sea. Her cargo consisted, as far as be could see, of oak and fir planks She seemed to have been deserted for a long time as her deck was quite slippery with moss, nli her hatches and upperworks, except the posts and roundhouse were gone, one anchor and cable was gone, one chain cable was on tin; deck and one anchor on the bow, and the roundhouse which was green painted, was quite destitute of any thing, except a boot, a sounding lead, a saw and a har- Tel ot sait beef, that had already begun to decay þÿ her sides were black, with a white streak and her rudder gone. The vessel seemed to have the appearance of being newlv built. þÿ Jn order to lose no time. Captain W. did not venture to take her in tow, although he might have brought her into an Irish port, as the wind was N E. and good weather, by placing a jury rudder, and taking her in tow ; but, in case of after accident to his own ship, such a step might have vieiated his insurance A

pole or plank had been erected in the roundhouse and there is every probability that the crew was saved. The alxive particulars were forwarded to the Underwriters of Lloyds, by Capt. Warming, from Funchal, Madeira.

The foreign and domestic intelligence of the week begins to assume new interest and importance with the re-assemblement of the parliament. In all the countries of Europe, aud m England in particular, the two houses, which form the Chambers of State, are at once the stage of political conflict, and the theatre of public business, and when these are closed by any interval of sessions or public holidays, the two houses are as it were shut up, and everything in the nature of interest or public occupation is cut off' till their reopening. In England, France, and Spain, these States are now in full sitting and occupation, and tlvere is no longer the former dearth, either of domestic or foreign intelligence. In France, the attention of the Chambers and the public mind are occupied with the very serious state of the French finances, and with the alarming deficit which the budget of every year exhibits between the enormous expenditure and the actual or expected revenue. From the public accounts which were rendered in the Chambers, it appears that the actual deficit amounts already to about a hundred millions of francs, or four millions English pounds sterling, which has all accumulated in about three years, being the deficit of the ordinary budgets of IS 10. 1841, and 1842. In the face of this enormous deficit, increas- i Great Britain lor the ing from year to year, the Chambers have j follows, viz had the imprudence to vote 140,000,000 j I francs, or 5,000,000/. In the House of Commons, after a new writ being ordered to issue for Nottingham, the business was com- . I rnenced by a question, whether there was any truth in the public report that a soldier of the I lib Hussars, Lord Cardigan's regi ment, had been flogged after Divine Service on Sunday. Mr. Macaulay replied, that the soldier had indeed been flogged on that day, but that the circumstances of the case had been somewhat incorrectly stated in the public prints. Instead of the punishment having followed immediately upon the conclusion of Divme Service, a long inspection had been 1 gone through before the troops were marched j back to tiie riding-, school, and it was not true that a portion of another regiment (the 14th) had been detained to witness the punishment. He entirely disapproved of the infliction of ! punishment on a Sunday, a practice which ) only urgent necessity þÿ such as in this case I did not exist þÿ could justify ; but such notice should he taken ol the case as would prevent J the recurrence of any similar one. Extract of a letter from a passenger on hoard the British Queen, outwaid bound, dated Halifax, Monday, March þÿ29: 1 he date ol my letter will a little surprise you Yet we are not arrived but if the present wind ami sea continue, we shall he at Halifax tomorrow. Nineteen davs and nights have J passed since J left Portsmouth, full of heart and health and hope. For two or three of these days all went smoothly, hut alas! for the 10 or 11 following, never shall I forget them. Our Ice paddles or floats, from some accident or mismanagement, began to drop off daily, until, on the 16tli instant, not one of them remained upon that wheel. At this period Providence gave us exactly six hours' calm, during which we look half the paddles from the starboard, and fixed them to the larboard wheel. That night we had a hurricane, which scarcely ceased or modcrated for 226 hours. The steam power ol the ship, crippled as she was, was totally iundcqnate to the size of her and the stmm We rolled helplessly in the mighty billows Eve-

þÿ ry sail was split into rags, and we were com I letely at the meicy of the waves. Oh! it was an awful time! I went not to lied for seveial nights, and had not my clothes <41 tor many My deck berth I was afraid toremain in 1 sat up in the main saloon. The rolling of the huge mass was terrific. From beam end to beam end the wa'ery mountains pitched her with fearful violence. Her paddle boxes and w bee's alone brought her up; hut how her timbers shook 1 Her sides rebounded. her hulk heads creaked, her rudder thumped, while the roaring of the storm was heard above all. One of our officers was injured; another was ill. The crew could hardly bear p weather, and were lashed. I, in the meanwhile, was in a nervous stale of terror, though the world saw it not We ought to have pushed for Fayal when our floats disappeared þÿ say when we were five or six davs out. I hinted this to the captain, hut he pressed onward into the great Atlantic, until the violence of the storm and size of the waves rendered it unsafe to send before the wind, and our only chance was to face it with half paddle power. The consequence was, we were twice (each time for four or five hours) in the trough of the sea without steerage wav, and as helpless as a raft þÿ Nothing saved us but the prodigious strength and buoyancy of our noble ship, whirh only wants 150 horse power more to make her unconquerable However, the danger, is, I hope, now passed. The wind is light, the sea smooth, we are passed Sable Island, and

within 18 hours of Halifax, at our present þÿsailing seven þÿknots all she ean do. We have some six oi seven þÿdays coal left, but aie prepared for another storm on a lee shore, and go in to r» fit and re fuel. It will prohably be a week or more ere we reach New York.

þÿ Wednesday. March 31. þÿ We got on shore last night, dreadfully cold, and gale from \ W with a snow storm, which covered our ship with ice, and from every thing in our rooms. We have no files on board, and some are frost bitten. To day tfie sun is shining, and 1 have been some hours wandering about this miserable town We leave to night at six or seven þÿo clock, hoping by that time to have our paddles ready and coals in. We have some 76 passengers of all kinds of nations, principally Germans, A motley uninteresting group they are. The foie cabin have been let loose upon the aft passengers, and turned the saloon into a beargarden. The race of this line of steamers i run. I have done with them for ever, li has been a miserable passage."

They appear to court a war with Great Britain ; but fortunately, the administration possess a decided majority in Congress m fa vor of peace, and Mr Webster was ably defended by his friends in the Senate It is plain that the Governor of the .State of New York has acted in opposition to the Genet al Government, in their endeavors to effect the release of McLeod. days from Bristol, and sailed again the lOih with 82 passengers. In her numerous trips across the Atlantic, she has never yet met with accident. Many floating rumours about the ill fated President are noticed in the papers, but they i have all proved unfounded.

The members ot the Council and Assembly were sworn in at noon, alter which Ihe Assembly proceeded to the election of Speaker Austin Ctivillier Esq. member ft.tr Huntingdon, was elected without opposition, the nomination of Sir Allan Mc'Nab being withdrawn, at bis own request. Mr. C nvillier is a merchant of Montreal, a French (Canadian. E li >tt until he could obtain the Emperot seontn mation o! it. The Imperial Cabinet, superficially acquainted with the emergency ot circumstances, lias rejected the treaty, and detei mined on war. Four Imperial edicts have been received, breathing hostility and defiance to the English, ordering that þÿ since the rebellious disposition of the foreigners has thus become manifest, nothing is left but to exterminate þÿthem. Instead of yielding an inrh by paying down the price of the opium, or granting them a landing-place, the Emperor describes the English as having rebelled against Heaven and opposed reason. 1 hey are, says he, þÿ like dogs and sheep j in th 'ir disposition It is difficult for heaven arui earth any lunger to hear with the English, ; and both Gods and men are indignant at their i þÿ Conduct. that for months past they "have debauched j | have þÿheard, says the Emperor, men's wives and daughters þÿ made captives carried away property þÿ built þÿforts opened watercourses, and set up a counterfeit public

officer, who issues proclamations ordering the people to pay the duties, in sleeping or eating, I find no þÿquiet. I he blood of the Tartar rulers is excited bv these enormities Keshen is ordered to he delivered over to the hoard of þÿ still, however, retaining his command ; and punishment the Admiral Kivan, though descended from have been ordered to proceed with all Troops i the god of war, is to lose his button. speed to Canton Flying orders have been sent to the provinces ol Honan, Achsen, and Kivei. Also, living despatches to Kean Ne, to forward the 2,000 troops already stationed at Kan Chow for Canton, and it is calculated that on the second moon of the year all the troops in succession may arrive at Canton. Keshen is ordered to exhort and stimulate the soldiers to advance with valorous daring, and to be foremost in battle, for it is þÿ absolutely necessary that the rebellions foreigners must give up their heads, which, and the prisoners, are to be sent to Pekin in cages to undergo the last þÿpenalty. An American gentleman, lately from Canton, tells us the city is doomed to the flames if we spare it. While we feel confident that any attempt on our part to eulogize the character of our late respected \dmiial would he almost super 1 fluous þÿ still weeannot retrain hunt expressing, hi some measure, those feelings which na ut ally press upon the mind from the melancholy reflection ot the awlully sudden death of one whose public services and private worth commanded the respect, and won the esteem of the community in which he lived.

Charles V. þÿ When Charles V, returned from Tunis he traveled by land through Calabria and to Naples, and did much good by the road At l,a Cava, the town council met to consider what present they should give the Emperor. Some were for pine-apples, the kernels of which are of a vast size ; but ihe majority carried it in favor of a kind of fig, winch they cover with mats in winterand in March, (the titne of the Emperor's passing) the fruit is very ripe, and delicious eating The Emperor received the deputies verv graciously; and expressing great sur prise at the fineness of the fruit at that season of the year inquired whether they eould pre- j serve anv quantity of them, and whether they were in abundance. þÿ Oh, said the wdse mavor, þÿ we have such plenty that we give them to our þÿhogs þÿWhat. said Charles, þÿ þÿ to vour hogs? þÿ then take your figs back again þÿ; and so saving, he flung a ripe one full in the face of the orator. The courtiers, following the example of their Sovereign, the poor deputies had their faces all besmeared and their eves bunged out w ith the fruit As they returned from the audience, one of these sapient senators, taking the whole to be part of the ceremonial of a reception by an emperor, observed to his brethren how lucky it was they had carried the point in favor of figs; for, had they presented pineapples, they would undoubtedly have had their brains knocked out. þÿ þÿSwinburne Courts s of Europe-

The Rogue forts which commanded the entrance of the Bocca Tigris, offered the most resistance ; a great many cannon had been placed in them and the Chi nese thought them impregnable; but while the ships and steamers attacked them in front, a considerable land force was landed in their rear, and thus surrounded, the garrisons surrendered after an þÿhour s cannonading. It is the first

time anv foreign vessel of war has ever been seen from the walls of Canton. The British also destroyed all their war junks, pursuing them into creeks where the Chinese thought they were oat of danger. THE PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE, Which was delivered to both houses of Congress yesterday at 12 o'clock at noon, was received in this city at hall' past SI o'clock in the evening;, and before 10 o'clock was in the hands of our compositors. This is the briefest space of time in which any message has been transmitted from Washington to New York.

From the National Intelligencer Extra, of June 1. This day the President of the United States transmitted to both Houses of Congress the following Atrsxfige. To the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States : Fellow Citizens : You have been assembled in your respective halls of legislation under a proclamation bearing the signature of the illustrious citizen who was so lately called by the diiect suffrages of the people to the discharge of the important functions ot their chief executive office. Upon the expiration of a single month from his installation, he has paid the great debt of nature, leaving behind him a name associated with the recollection of numerous benefits conferred upon the country during a long life of patriotic devotion. With this public bereavement a rb connected other considerations which will not escape the attention of Congress. The preparations necessary for his removal to the seat of Government in view of a residence of four years must have devolved upon the late Piesident heavy expenditures, which, if permitted to burden the limited resources of his private fortune, may tend seriously to the embarrassment of his surviving familv ; and it is therefore respectfully submitted to Congress whether the ordinary principles of justice would not dictate the propriety of its legislative interposition By the provisions of the fundamental law, the powers and duties of the high station to which he was elected have devolved upon me, and in the dispositions of the representa-

tives of the states and of the people will be found to a great extent a solution of llie problem to which our institutions are for the lirst time subjected. In entering upon the duties of this office, I did not feel that it would be becoming in me to disturb what had been ordered by my lamented predecessor. Whatever therefore may have been my opinion, originally, as to the propriety ot convening Congressat soearly a day from that of its late adjournment, I found a new and a controlling inducement not to interfere with the patriotic desires of the late President, in the novelty of the situation in which 1 was so unexpectedly placed. My first wish, under such circumstances, would necessarily have been to have called to my aid, in the administration of public affairs, the combined wisdom of the two Houses ot'Congress, inorder to taketheircounsel and advice as to the best mode of extricaling the government and the country from the embarrassments weighing heavily on both. 1 am then most happy in finding myself, so soon after my accession to the Presidency, surrounded by the immediate representatives of the states and people.

From the Furopean, June 19, 1841. We are just on the eve of a general election inGreat Britain and business is. therefore, though the prospects of trade have latterly been much brighter than heretofore, almost completely at a stand still. The dissolution, there is every reason to believe, will he gazetted on Tuesday next, after her Majesty has prorogued the parliament in person. Writs for a general election will then be forthwith issued to the several sheriffs for counties, who must within two days cause proclamation to be made of county electionsand must fix them to take place not sooner than the tenth nor later than the sixteenth day from the date of the proclamation. The sheriffs must also, within three davs from the receipt of the w rit, issue their precepts to the returning officers of the cities and boroughs, who must instantly cause proclamation to be made of the elections, and proceed to election thereon not sooner than four davs nor later than eight days from the date of the proclamation. The new parliament will meet forthwith after the elections, the votes of supply having been only taken for six months from the first of April. There are a thousand rumours in currency as to the result of this appeal to the nation ; but nine hundred and ninety nine of them are not worth notice. The only one to be credited is that ministers do not expect anything like a majority, but have made up their minds to a minority of from 30 to 40. The first trial of strength will most probably be on ihe speakership, as>

though Mr Lefevre is very much esteemed by all parties, jtlie conservative leader is too long-headed to throw away a chance. It is not however believed that ministers will resign in the event of a defeat on that point. The policy of the conservative party w ill then continue aggressive until their end shall he accomplished. A great many peers will be made before the ministers leave office. Ihe Crown Prince of Hanover (Prince George of Cumberland) has irrecoverably lost the sight of both eyes. On Wednesday a court of directors was held at the East India house, when Major General Sir Hugh Gough K C. 13 , was appointed commander in chief of the company's forces on the Madras establishment. l.ord J lius«ell will, we understand, shortly form a matrimonial alliance with the second daughter of the Earl and Countess of Minto. His Lordship is in his 49th, and the lady in her 26th year. We understand that the instructions given to Sir Henrv Pottinger, on proceeding as commissioner to Canton to supersede Captain Elliot, were warlike against the Chinese to an extreme degree. Failure in þÿLondon. þÿ The stoppage of Messrs. Cockburn and Co. the East India and Australian agents, of Old Broadstreet, has caused some alarm among the parties immediately connected iri their circle of business, inasmuch as it is apprehended that the cause which rendered this step necessary on their part will produce similar effects in other quarters. Their debts and liabilities are variously stated from £l 50.000 to £200.000 against which they

are understood to hold a large amount of produce which, if sold in the present state of the market. must pass at a ruinous sacrifice. The extensive commercial house of Grant and Co , of Glasgow, have failed ; their liabilities are said to amount to £180,000, and it is feared the effect will be felt bv many other houses. It is stated that the very important event of the accouchement of her majesty is expected at the latter end of September, or earh in October.

This decision will either order his liberation under the laws of nations, or his trial according to the laws of this State. 1 he whole difficulty grows out of the different views taken by the General and the -State Governments. Ihe annexed correspondence between the Governor of New York and the President of the United States, which has never \et been published, indicate this position. Executive Department, ) Albany, May 4, 1841. \ Sir þÿ I have just learned liom the public prints that the Disinct Attorney ol the United States for the Northern District of New Yoik. is in attendance upon the Supreme Court of this State, in behalf of Alexander McLeod who is indicted for murder committed in the "destruction" of the boat "Caroline," and which indictment is pending in the courts of this State. As the Attorney General of this State, and the District Attorney of Niagara county, have charge of this prosecution in behalf of the people of the state of New Y"rk; the unseemly aspect is presented of a conflict between the f ederal Government and that of this State, which 1 respectfully submit to vou, is not calculated to inspire confidence among

the common constituents of both in the harmonious relations and views of the two governments, nor to challenge that respect from Great Britain to which our institutions are entitled, and which it is so essential to preserve, particularly in the present state of the controversy with her. 1 am sure 1 need do no more than call your attention to the subject, to insure such a dts position of it, as will manifest the regard which there can be no doubt of your entertaming for the rights and character of this State, in the conduct of a prosecution for an offence against her sovereignty. Very respectfully, Your obedient servant, WILLIAM H. SEWAKD. The President of the United Slates.

The President of the U. Stales to the. Governor, Washington. May 7th, 1841 þÿSir I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your Excellency's letter of the 4th inst. in which you are pleased to say, that, "you have just learned from the public prints that the District Attorney of the United Slates for the Northern District of New York, is in attendance on the Supreme Court of this Slate, (New York) in behalf of Alexander McLeod. who is indicted for murder committed in the destruction of the boat Caroline, and which indictment is pending in the Supreme Court of this State." and that '« as the Attorney General of this State, and the District Attorney of Niagara county, have charge of the prosecution in behalf of the people of the State of New York, the unseemly aspect is presented of a conflict between the Federal

Government and that of this State, which I respectfully submit to you is not calculated to inspire confidence among the common constituents of both in the harmonious relation and views of the two governments, nor to challenge that respect from Great Britain to which our institutions are entitled, and which it is so essential to preserve, particularly in the present state of the controversy with her." In reply, I have the honor to say, that the District Attorney of the United States for the Northern District of New York, has received no orders from this Government to appear as counsel in defence of McLeod þÿ nor can 1 believe that in the absence of such orders, he has undertak n to assume that task in his official character. So far as I am informed Mr. Spencer acts entirely in his private rapa. city as a practising attorney of the State of New York, in consequence of a retainer which dates hack from a period antecedent to his having had official station conferred upon him I am sure that in this you will see nothing unseemly, or calculated either to encourage a belief of the want of liarinonv in the rela'ions or views ol the two governments, or in any way to diminish the respect of any foreign government for our institutions. This I government has done no more in reference to the trial to be had before the Supreme Courts of New York, than to furnish the counsel for the accused, upon their requisition, with such documentary evidence as was to be found in the Department, and which was believed bv

them to be accessary to be used in the defence In giving your Excellency the foregoing explanation. I am not to be understood as deriving to this government, in order to the fulfilment of its international duties and obligations, the right to resort to all constitutional and legitimate means within its power. The confidence which 1 feel in the learning and justice of the Supreme Court of New Y ork, and in the tribunals instituted bv her for dispensing full and perfect justice, would cause me to avoid the commission of any act which would bear a doubtful construction. I pray your Excellency to arcrpt assurances of my high consideration and respect. JOHN TYLER. Ilis Excellency Wm. H. Seward.

þÿoco-«» London, June 3, 1841. Political parties are undergoing a fresh organization in this country. For a time the term whig and torv is suspended, and free traders or monopolist is the ticket. Still the latter class does not lose quite so much of its force as the whigs, as the tories aie to a man selfish, and only regard class interests, whilst a portion of the whigs admit the passions of the masses should be respected. Our glorious constitution is now brought to a pretty pass þÿ and its clumsiness is becoming more manifest each dav. We hear the full toned words of King, Lords, and Commons, but when we try to unite such discordant elements, we find they act with no harmony. At this present moment, we may he said to be þÿ without a government the ministers of the crown arc powerless Now such a nation as England, with the functions of its government suspended, must present an awkward feature to constitutional monarch þÿ but so it is The theory of our constitution proclaims the powers of the government to be suspended and defunct, when its ministers

do not possess the confidence of the House of Commons þÿ and such is the case at this time þÿ the Melbnurn ministry has sustained several defeats, and yet it is too tenacious of office, and has too murh regard for the welfare of the masses to give up the executive to the Tories. Sir Robert Feci prescribes this conduct, and denounces it unconstitutional þÿ and he barks his proposition þÿ by a reference to many precedents, as far back as 1740 þÿ and at various subsequent dates when the ministers of the crown did resign their authority and power, when i hey found that the confidence of the House of Commons had left them. Here is the leader of the conservative partv, attempting to establish an analogy-bet ween the present time and the good old days of boroughmongering. is it not ridiculous. The whigs will not resign þÿ they will appeal to the people. The debate on want of confidence still continues. The excitement is unabated on the corn Jaw ; every day the discussion is prolonged, gives strength to the repealers. One fact was elicited a few nights since, on the presentation of a petition for the repeal of the corn law in the Lords þÿ when it was remarked by the Earl of Radnor, that every article of sustenance was prohibited bv heavy import duties þÿ except turbnt and lobsters, two expressive fish, which could only reach the table of the aristocracy. The noble Lords look very crabbed at this coarse impertinence, and denounced the fact as it tended to cast an im-

putation on the most exalted body of men in any assembly of this world. The House of Lords stumps creation. A good deal of difficulty is now experienced in taking the census of our population. The tories have inflamed the minds of the people against such returns, and the ignorance is so strong that a majority of the lower classes refuse filling up the papers left at each house for that purpose, as they consider it an infringement on the rights of the British subject. A social revolution is taking plaee in Ireland þÿ it will soon lose all its blarney and poetical aspirations, by the hand of temperance.
